core: schedule as a time-based planning representation
supporting: distinguishing a schedule from a task list
outOfScope: cost, procurement, legal, or staffing advice

claims.claim: Project scheduling is a distinct project-management practice, and PMI publishes a dedicated scheduling practice standard alongside project standards and guides.
A usable schedule represents planned work in time; it is more informative than an unordered list because it gives activities and key events temporal placement.
Duration estimates depend on the information and assumptions available and should be treated as estimates rather than promises.
A milestone is a significant point or event in a schedule and can make a review or decision point visible without itself describing all the work around it.
A schedule baseline is an approved version of a schedule model that can be compared with actual performance; the comparison does not by itself explain or solve a variance.
Updating a schedule in light of actual progress and changed assumptions can improve the quality of the current forecast, but does not remove uncertainty or guarantee delivery on a date.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Scheduling references often describe sophisticated network, resource, and performance-control methods, while this introductory topic has a narrower purpose.
positions: PMI identifies scheduling as a substantial professional practice area.
GAO describes detailed schedule-development and updating practices for government cost-estimation contexts.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses those sources only to support general concepts of time-based planning, estimates, milestones, baseline comparison, and uncertainty. It does not teach calculations, mandate a tool, or prescribe a government process.

unsupportedExistingClaims: A generic draft could mistake a date list for a schedule, present one estimate as certain, or imply that a schedule baseline makes the future fixed.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic content with original instruction distinguishing activities, durations, milestones, and baselines.
Used a labeled hypothetical example and explicitly retained uncertainty rather than promising a delivery result.
rightsIssues: PMI materials were read live and are treated as REFERENCE_ONLY; no source prose, charts, templates, or standards text was reproduced.
The GAO guide was read live and is treated as a public-domain government source; this lesson uses original prose and no source figures or tables.
